nodes.label: Romila Thapar
nodes.date_label: Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961) · From Lineage to State (1984) · Somanatha: The Many Voices of a History (2004) · The Past before Us (2013) · History as a Way of Remembering the Past (2014) · The Past as Present: Lahore keynote (2015)
nodes.description: A historian of early India who joined textual and material evidence to questions of social change. The Library of Congress’s 2008 assessment emphasizes that methodological shift. In her 2014 methods chapter she distinguishes historical consciousness from conformity to modern European genres. Her 2015 Lahore lecture challenges inherited religious divisions of Indian history and reconstructs the changing uses of the Somanatha narrative. Talbot’s review presents The Past before Us as a study of the social purposes served by perceptions of the past. These are distinct inquiries, not a claim that every premodern narrative is reliable history.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Asoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (1961); From Lineage to State (1984); Somanatha (2004); The Past before Us (2013); History as a Way of Remembering the Past (2014); The Past as Present (Lahore keynote, 2015).
nodes.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-24: the Library of Congress assessment; Thapar’s 2015 speech; her 2014 publisher excerpt at pp. 21–24; the displayed opening extracts of Talbot’s 2014 and Veluthat’s 2004 reviews. Books are unread; the 1961 and 1984 titles are catalogue-only. The 2015 speech is not the similarly titled 2014 essay collection. Later work and reception have not been surveyed; no career ending is asserted.

nodes.label: Cheikh Anta Diop
nodes.date_label: Nations nègres et culture (1954) · Les fondements économiques et culturels d’un futur État fédéral en Afrique noire (1960) · Antériorité des civilisations nègres (1967) · Civilisation ou barbarie (1981)
nodes.description: A Senegalese historian whose restoration of African historical consciousness connected Egypt, cultural continuity and Pan-African political projects. Tine distinguishes his programme from Senghor’s négritude and reports Dieng’s objections to its treatment of nationhood and cultural borrowing. Diop’s propositions about Egypt and cultural diffusion remain attributed and contested; neither a common African essence nor agreement among African historians is asserted.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Nations nègres et culture (1954); Les fondements économiques et culturels d’un futur État fédéral en Afrique noire (1960); Antériorité des civilisations nègres (1967); Civilisation ou barbarie (1981).
nodes.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-24: Tine’s introduction, section 2 and conclusion in an author-authorized repository; the publisher’s search-rendered account; BnF/INHA metadata; UCAD’s centenary programme metadata. Diop’s books and Dieng’s original critiques are unread. Claims from 1981 and 1989 are mediated through Tine. No verdict on the population of ancient Egypt is established by publisher praise or a commemorative programme. Tine’s death-year error is excluded; UCAD gives 1986. Original French titles and later translations are not conflated.

nodes.label: Liang Qichao
nodes.date_label: An Introduction to Chinese History (1901) · New Historiography (Xin shixue) (1902) · Observations on a Trip to America (1903) · Outline of Scholarship in the Qing Dynasty (1920) · Nankai lectures on methods of Chinese historical research (1921)
nodes.description: A reform-era Chinese scholar whose historiographical programme moved beyond dynastic court narratives toward histories of people and social change. Civic renewal in his authorized translated text combines inherited resources with selective borrowing. Blitstein shows that Liang’s 1920 account of Qing scholarship recovered a Chinese intellectual renewal, while Hu Shi used renaissance differently. Dirlik credits Liang’s break with older historical writing but questions its explanatory framework. These shifts prevent treating his lifetime’s work as one unchanging nationalist doctrine.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: An Introduction to Chinese History (1901); New Historiography/Xin shixue (1902); Renewing the People (selected translated text); Observations on a Trip to America (1903); Outline of Scholarship in the Qing Dynasty/Qingdai xueshu gailun (written 1920); Nankai historical-method lectures (1921).
nodes.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-24: authorized Columbia translations of selected writings; Dirlik’s introduction and epilogue passages; Blitstein pp. 180–182; Zheng’s relevant historical discussion. The 1902 and 1920 works are known through named academic readers, not newly read in Chinese. The 1921 milestone dates lectures, without conflating them with later editions of Chinese historical research methods. Blitstein’s 2021 issue date is distinct from 2020 online/copyright metadata. No direct relation to individual European thinkers is inferred from resemblance.

nodes.label: Gu Jiegang
nodes.date_label: Letters on the layering of ancient historical traditions (1923) · Gushibian volume1 and autobiographical preface (1926) · Edition of Cui Dongbi/Cui Shu’s writings (1936) · The Chinese Nation Is One (1939) · Index of the Shangshu (1962)
nodes.description: A Chinese historian, philologist and folklorist who examined the accumulated layers of ancient historical traditions rather than treating transmitted narratives as transparent records. Richter describes both his 1923 critique of unitary origins and his recovery of earlier Chinese source criticism. The relation between that scepticism and his 1939 national-unity thesis remains contested: Jenco reads an open political community, whereas Kim and Zheng stress homogenizing limits. Dirlik reports contemporary Marxist objections to restricting criticism to documents; Lu questions aspects of Gu’s source chronology.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Stratification correspondence (1923); editor, Gushibian (from 1926); autobiographical preface (1926; Arthur W.Hummel’s English translation 1931); edition of Cui Dongbi/Cui Shu (1936); The Chinese Nation Is One (1939); Shangshu index (1962).
nodes.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-24: Richter’s complete 1982 obituary and the opening/references of her separate China Quarterly article; PKU biography; Lu’s Chinese/English abstracts; Jenco’s publisher abstract; Kim’s English abstract; Zheng’s Gu discussion; Dirlik’s selected epilogue passages. Gu’s original works remain unread. Chinese intellectual and philological traditions are not treated as mere imports of European methods. The 1926 series start is supported by Richter’s references; her obituary’s 1927 date is retained here as a source discrepancy, not silently harmonized. Jenco’s and Kim’s divergent interpretations remain attributed.

nodes.label: Ibn Khaldun
nodes.date_label: First Muqaddimah draft (1377) · Composition and revision of the larger Kitab al-Ibar in Tunis (1378–1382) · Final dated material in the surviving autobiography (1405)
nodes.description: A fourteenth-century historian formed within the intellectual and political worlds of the Islamic West. The Muqaddimah’s methodological introduction tests historical reports against social and political conditions. Its analysis of solidarity and authority offers a comparative question for historical sociology without making him a displaced modern European founder. Simon distinguishes the initial draft, later work on the larger history, and the surviving autobiography. Hannoum’s 2026 reading places colonial remakings alongside earlier Islamic receptions, keeping the transmission of his work a historical problem in its own right.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Muqaddimah (first draft November 1377); Kitab al-Ibar (larger-history composition/revision in Tunis 1378–1382); autobiography/at-Taʿrif (surviving continuation throughMay 1405). Modern reception is dated separately.
nodes.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-24: selected pages of Princeton’s translated author-text excerpt; Simon pp. 64–65 and 99–103; Stanford section 15; Hannoum’s selected sections. The Arabic originals and the larger history/autobiography themselves are unread; their writing chronology is mediated through Simon. Three separate writing milestones are shown, without turning modern translations into original contributions or assigning an invented single publication date. The 1405 point marks the final dated autobiographical material, not a confidently dated completion. Modern field comparisons do not establish direct intellectual descent, and this entry does not stand for all Islamic historiography.

nodes.label: Masao Maruyama
nodes.date_label: Essays later collected as Studies in the Intellectual History of Tokugawa Japan (1940–1944) · Logic and Mentality of Ultra-Nationalism (1946) · Japanese Thought (1957) · Approach to Intellectual History (1960) · Reading of Outline of Civilization Theory (1986)
nodes.description: A historian of Japanese political thought whose Tokugawa studies and postwar writings asked how intellectual change and political responsibility become possible. His 1946 analysis of ultranationalism, 1957 account of historical consciousness and 1960 reflection on intellectual history are read here through Nakajima. Nakajima also criticizes the colonial exclusions of his democratic nationalism; Lim questions the deterministic account of China in the Tokugawa studies. The existing comparison with modernization theory remains a comparison of questions, not an affiliation.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: Studies in the Intellectual History of Tokugawa Japan (essays 1940–44; Japanese collection 1952; English translation by Mikiso Hane 1974); Logic and Mentality of Ultra-Nationalism (1946); Japanese Thought (original essay 1957; later collected separately); Approach to Intellectual History (1960); Thought and Behaviour in Modern Japanese Politics (English 1963; expanded 1969); Reading of Outline of Civilization Theory (1986).
nodes.scope_note: Read on 2026-10-24: Nakajima’s selected chapter pages and Lim’s English abstract; NDL catalogue metadata. The original Japanese essays and 1986 commentary remain unread, known through named readers. The prior source’s narrower primary-opening review is retained, including its caution about the platform’s 1989 reissue description. The 1952 collection, 1974 translation and 1940–44 essays are distinct. Existing person ID and intellectual-history roster wording are preserved.
